arbeitssicherheit-all.title: Workplace safety – fundamentals for staff and management
arbeitssicherheit-all.description: Five lessons moving from the legal architecture of the Arbeitsschutzgesetz through the annual training duty under DGUV Vorschrift 1, to risk assessment, personal protective equipment, emergency preparedness, and display-screen workstations. Designed as recurring mandatory training – DGUV Vorschrift 1 requires instruction at least once a year, which the second lesson covers directly.

arbeitssicherheit-l1.title: Who owes whom what? Basic duties under the ArbSchG

arbeitssicherheit-l1-s1.title: The employer's basic duty – and who may carry it
arbeitssicherheit-l1-s1.body: §3(1) ArbSchG requires the employer to take the occupational-safety measures necessary for employees' safety and health, taking into account the circumstances affecting their safety and health at work. This is not a one-off duty: §3(1) explicitly requires measures to be checked for effectiveness and adapted to changing conditions, and §3(2) requires a suitable organisational structure and the necessary resources. This basic duty sits with the employer in the first instance – §7 additionally requires the employer to take employees' qualifications and prior instruction into account when assigning tasks. §13(2) further allows the employer's occupational-safety tasks to be delegated in writing to reliable, competent persons, but responsibility for making sure such a delegation system actually works stays with the employer.

arbeitssicherheit-l1-s2.title: Employee duties – not a one-way street
arbeitssicherheit-l1-s2.body: Occupational safety is not purely an employer duty. §15(1) ArbSchG obliges every employee, to the extent of their own ability and in line with the employer's instruction and directions, to take care of their own safety and health at work – and equally of the safety and health of other persons affected by their acts or omissions at work. §16 spells this out further: machinery, tools, hazardous substances and personal protective equipment must be used as intended, and any immediate significant danger or defect in protective systems must be reported to the employer or the responsible person without delay. This duty to cooperate is the flip side of the instruction duty covered in Lesson 2: without it, even the best instruction has no effect.

arbeitssicherheit-l2.title: Why you're here: the annual training duty

arbeitssicherheit-l2-s1.title: §12 ArbSchG plus §4 DGUV Vorschrift 1: a hard recurring duty
arbeitssicherheit-l2-s1.body: §12(1) ArbSchG requires the employer to give employees sufficient and appropriate instruction on safety and health at work – in particular on recruitment, on changes to their area of responsibility, and when new work equipment or new technology is introduced, tailored to each employee's actual workplace and tasks. The statute names these triggers but leaves the question of "how often" relatively open. That is exactly where §4(1) DGUV Vorschrift 1 steps in and turns it into a hard number: employers must instruct insured persons as needed, but at least once a year, on the accident and health hazards arising from their work and on the measures and facilities in place to avert those hazards. "At least once a year" is therefore not a recommendation but a binding accident-prevention regulation (Unfallverhütungsvorschrift) of the statutory accident insurance system – and it is why this course is designed as a recurring mandatory training, regardless of your role in the company.

arbeitssicherheit-l2-s2.title: More than the annual date: triggers, evidence, audience
arbeitssicherheit-l2-s2.body: The annual minimum instruction is the floor, not the entire duty. §12(1) ArbSchG also requires additional, trigger-based instruction – for new employees, on a change of role, when new work equipment or technology is introduced – and in practice also after near-misses or a noticeably changed hazard picture. Shorter intervals or special requirements apply to certain groups, for example minors or particularly hazardous tasks; the specific timeframes for those cases sit in dedicated special rules and are deliberately not given a number here. §12(2) ArbSchG also makes clear that instruction must take place during working hours and be repeated where necessary. Whether instruction actually happened – who, when, on what content – can generally only be proven in a dispute or an inspection if it was documented; even though the exact scope of documentation is not spelled out in every detail by statute, keeping a written or electronic record is treated as indispensable in workplace practice.

arbeitssicherheit-l3.title: Risk assessment: a duty before every measure

arbeitssicherheit-l3-s1.title: Assess first, act second
arbeitssicherheit-l3-s1.body: §5(1) ArbSchG requires the employer to determine, through an assessment of the hazards employees face in their work, which occupational-safety measures are necessary. This risk assessment is therefore not an optional add-on document but the statutory precondition for practically everything else in this course: it is what determines what actually needs to be covered in instruction (Lesson 2), what personal protective equipment is required (Lesson 4), and what requirements a specific display-screen workstation must meet (Lesson 5). §5(3) gives a non-exhaustive list of possible hazard sources for this purpose – from the design and layout of the workplace, to physical, chemical and biological effects, the design of work and production processes, insufficient qualification and instruction, through to psychological strain at work. Importantly, under §3(1) a risk assessment is not a one-off exercise; it must be reviewed and adapted whenever circumstances change – new equipment, new processes, or after an accident.

arbeitssicherheit-l3-s2.title: Documentation: the result must be traceable
arbeitssicherheit-l3-s2.body: §6(1) ArbSchG requires the employer to compile the necessary documentation on the results of the risk assessment, the occupational-safety measures determined by the employer, and the results of their review – in a form and to an extent appropriate to the type of activities and the number of employees. For example: in an office with display-screen workstations, the risk assessment will typically cover ergonomic factors (Lesson 5), lighting and fire safety (Lesson 4), and psychological strain factors; in a workshop using machinery, mechanical, electrical and substance-related hazards are added on top. The precise scope of the documentation duty – including possible simplified forms for smaller businesses – depends on the concrete circumstances and is deliberately not given a blanket figure here; as a rule of thumb, the more traceable the documentation, the more it will hold up to a supervisory authority or in a dispute.

arbeitssicherheit-l4.title: Protective equipment and emergencies: when it counts

arbeitssicherheit-l4-s1.title: Personal protective equipment is the last line of defence
arbeitssicherheit-l4-s1.body: §4 No. 5 ArbSchG sets out one of the general principles of occupational safety: individual protective measures rank behind other measures. In practice, this means personal protective equipment (PPE) should only be used once technical and organisational measures cannot sufficiently eliminate or reduce the hazard – it is the last line of defence, not the first. Where the risk assessment from Lesson 3 shows PPE is required, the employer must select suitable equipment under the PSA-Benutzungsverordnung and provide it to employees free of charge. On the other side sits the employees' duty to use it: §15(2) ArbSchG requires them to use the personal protective equipment provided to them as intended. Provision without use – and use without provision – protects nobody.

arbeitssicherheit-l4-s2.title: Escape routes, fire safety and first aid: preparing before the emergency
arbeitssicherheit-l4-s2.body: The Technical Rules for Workplaces (ASR) flesh out the Arbeitsstättenverordnung with requirements that matter in an emergency. ASR A2.3 requires clearly marked escape routes and emergency exits that must be kept clear at all times, with their number, width and length depending on usage, dimensions and the number of people present. ASR A2.2 requires measures against fire, including suitable and sufficient fire-extinguishing equipment and escape/rescue plans where the type of use calls for them. For medical emergencies, §26 DGUV Vorschrift 1 requires the employer to ensure a sufficient number of trained first-aiders; the exact number depends on workplace factors such as headcount and hazard profile and is deliberately not given a blanket figure here. DGUV Information 204-022 further describes the first-aid equipment – such as first-aid kits – that a workplace should keep on hand. Important for every employee: knowing where these facilities are is part of the instruction covered in Lesson 2, not a separate topic.

arbeitssicherheit-l5.title: Display-screen workstations: ergonomics is not optional

arbeitssicherheit-l5-s1.title: What Annex No. 6 ArbStättV expects of a display-screen workstation
arbeitssicherheit-l5-s1.body: Annex No. 6 of the Arbeitsstättenverordnung sets concrete minimum requirements for display-screen workstations that follow from the risk assessment for this type of workplace: the screen must be free of disturbing flicker and reflections, and adjustable in tilt and viewing distance; the keyboard must be separate from the screen and tiltable, to allow a hand position that avoids fatigue; the work surface and chair must allow sufficient freedom of movement and a healthy posture; lighting must be adequate and must not create disturbing glare or reflections on the screen. The Annex also sets requirements for the software used – among other things, it must be suited to the task being carried out and designed to be user-friendly. These are not design suggestions but legally binding minimum requirements against which a specific workstation can, if in doubt, be checked.

arbeitssicherheit-l5-s2.title: The eye-test entitlement: an offer, not a requirement
arbeitssicherheit-l5-s2.body: Annex Part 4 of the Ordinance on Occupational Health Care (ArbMedVV) classifies display-screen work as an activity subject to so-called "offered" health surveillance (Angebotsvorsorge): the employer must offer employees who regularly work at display screens an occupational health check – including an eye and vision examination – before they start the activity and at regular intervals afterwards. The key distinction from mandatory health surveillance is that employees may accept or decline the offer; there is no requirement to take it up. If the examination shows that normal vision aids are not sufficient for display-screen work, the employer must provide special vision aids for that work. The specific interval at which the offer must be repeated depends on medical assessment, and is therefore deliberately not given as a fixed number of years here.
